all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: rendering
concepts.definition: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.

defining_facts.text: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.
In the context of creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the terms view or rendering are used in a broad sense to refer not only to visual output but also to output for other senses.

From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.

Rendering, the key component of any immersive experience in which the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device, is covered by computer graphics, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.

concepts.name: computer graphics
concepts.definition: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.

defining_facts.text: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.

One possibility for creating a virtual world is texture mapping, in which camera images of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object; this is a common computer-graphics operation that virtual reality (VR) software should ideally support.

For a good virtual reality (VR) immersive experience, client-end hardware is needed to support requirements arising from rendering or computer graphics and to manage rendering or computer graphics related issues, and the complexity required to render a scene corresponds to the need for high-end hardware support.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.
The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to create or represent objects, synthesize objects into a scene, and render the scene on a computer display so that humans can perceive it.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: clipping
concepts.definition: Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality.

defining_facts.text: Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality.
Clipping is the process of discarding objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume, and it takes place before projection.

To project a point P from the world coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view plane, P is first transformed to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, then the view volume containing P is transformed to a canonical view volume before clipping, and finally the point in the canonical view volume is projected onto the view plane; the final point P' is obtained by multiplying P by the world coordinate system to three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system transformation matrix, the canonical view volume transformation matrix, and the projection transformation matrix.

Clipping defines a view volume, discards objects or portions of objects outside that view volume, and is performed before projection so that projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced.

concepts.name: pixel
concepts.definition: A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

defining_facts.text: A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.
In a raster scan device, the light emitted from excited pixel elements decays over time, causing the rendered scene to fade even when the image is not changing.

In raster scan rendering, pixels are excited in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order, so the top-left pixel is excited much earlier than the bottom-right pixel; because the emitted light decays, pixels may fade out of sync and the displayed image may appear non-uniform or distorted.
Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels on a raster scan device, done to avoid fading and distortion and to keep the rendered image uniform even when the image is not changing.

In a color display, each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three although sometimes four can be used for different purposes; the typical three elements emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities.

Color is perceived when the red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display is mixed in the eye, so the observed color is a combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue.

concepts.name: edge
concepts.definition: The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.

defining_facts.text: The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.

concepts.name: display controller
concepts.definition: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

defining_facts.text: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.
The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU.
The display controller generates the image in a digital format, as strings of zeros and ones, and sends that image representation to video memory for storage.

concepts.name: video controller
concepts.definition: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

defining_facts.text: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

concepts.name: frame buffer
concepts.definition: In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

defining_facts.text: In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.
The size of a frame buffer is the size of the screen and is equal to the screen resolution of a raster scan device.

never_defined.name: computer vision technique
never_defined.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications are more versatile than marker-based augmented reality applications, do not require physical markers, can use computer vision techniques, and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional space
never_defined.definition: In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

never_defined.name: input sensor
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the processing part or computer is a device that processes data from input sensors and, based on that processing, activates or actuates output devices.

never_defined.name: point
never_defined.definition: In natural feature tracking, the advanced image processing algorithms or computer vision techniques detect features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked, such as points, corners, and line intersections.

never_defined.name: surface
never_defined.definition: Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

never_defined.name: animation
never_defined.definition: Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior, with capabilities ranging from scene construction only to the full capability of building complex interactive behavior.

never_defined.name: stage
never_defined.definition: A software development lifecycle is a set of stages that should ideally be followed in a particular sequence.

never_defined.name: vertex
never_defined.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

never_defined.name: curve
never_defined.definition: Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived.

never_defined.name: color value
never_defined.definition: The color values stored in the frame buffer are computed by the display processor, which is part of the display controller, in distinct stages.

never_defined.name: display processor
never_defined.definition: The color values stored in the frame buffer are computed by the display processor, which is part of the display controller, in distinct stages.

never_defined.name: display mechanism
never_defined.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional view coordinate system
never_defined.definition: Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional view coordinate system
never_defined.definition: Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional object representation technique
never_defined.definition: A single three-dimensional (3D) object representation technique is not sufficient because different object representation techniques are available, and the appropriate technique must be chosen for a particular problem.

never_defined.name: parametric representation
never_defined.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

never_defined.name: implicit representation
never_defined.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

never_defined.name: octree method
never_defined.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

never_defined.name: binary space partitioning method
never_defined.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

never_defined.name: constructive solid geometry method
never_defined.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

never_defined.name: data point
never_defined.definition: Point sample rendering is the simplest broad representation category, in which the captured scene information is represented as a set of raw data points on the scene, with each point carrying that information as attributes.

never_defined.name: attribute
never_defined.definition: Point sample rendering is the simplest broad representation category, in which the captured scene information is represented as a set of raw data points on the scene, with each point carrying that information as attributes.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional range scanner
never_defined.definition: In point sample rendering, the scene information is captured from the real world in the form of points using input sensors such as three-dimensional (3D) range scanners, range finders, or computer vision techniques.

never_defined.name: range finder
never_defined.definition: In point sample rendering, the scene information is captured from the real world in the form of points using input sensors such as three-dimensional (3D) range scanners, range finders, or computer vision techniques.

never_defined.name: synthetic image
never_defined.definition: In point sample rendering, the captured points are processed or mapped to pixels to generate a synthetic image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.

never_defined.name: polygon
never_defined.definition: Boundary representation is a broad representation category in which objects are represented by the surfaces that define the object's boundary, and those surfaces can be polygonal or curved.

never_defined.name: vertex list
never_defined.definition: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

never_defined.name: edge list
never_defined.definition: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

never_defined.name: triangle
never_defined.definition: Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used.

never_defined.name: simple convex polygon
never_defined.definition: Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used.

never_defined.name: pipeline
never_defined.definition: Mesh representation is the most basic form of representation for any object in a rendered scene used in computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to a mesh representation at the end of the pipeline before the objects are rendered.

never_defined.name: curved surface
never_defined.definition: Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curved surfaces or curves that falls under parametric representation.

never_defined.name: simple polygon
never_defined.definition: Spline representation is typically preferred by developers or designers of scenes who want to create an artificial environment, and it is used to construct quality scenes for rendering and to represent complex surfaces with complex properties that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.

never_defined.name: polynomial equation
never_defined.definition: Spline representation is typically preferred by developers or designers of scenes who want to create an artificial environment, and it is used to construct quality scenes for rendering and to represent complex surfaces with complex properties that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.

never_defined.name: polynomial
never_defined.definition: In polynomial representation of a curve, a more complex curve is represented by a polynomial of higher degree, and computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming.

never_defined.name: curve segment
never_defined.definition: In spline representation, a complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree complex polynomial, and each piece is called a blending function or basis function so that simpler polynomials can compute points on the curve segment represented by that piece.

never_defined.name: third-order polynomial
never_defined.definition: Third-order polynomials are the most common form of polynomial used to construct spline curves.

never_defined.name: spline curve
never_defined.definition: Third-order polynomials are the most common form of polynomial used to construct spline curves.

never_defined.name: binary space partitioning
never_defined.definition: Space partitioning representations include the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods.

never_defined.name: constructive solid geometry
never_defined.definition: Space partitioning representations include the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods.

never_defined.name: computer animation
never_defined.definition: A skeletal model is a specialized representation method for complex characters such as a cat that captures the character's overall appearance and motion behavior, and such models are typically used in animation or computer animation to represent objects or complex characters.

never_defined.name: pipeline stage
never_defined.definition: In an implementation of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, all pipeline stages are present, the stages are more important than their sequence, and the order of the stages and sub-stages may differ from the stage-wise sequence used to show how the computations occur.

never_defined.name: sub-stage
never_defined.definition: In an implementation of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, all pipeline stages are present, the stages are more important than their sequence, and the order of the stages and sub-stages may differ from the stage-wise sequence used to show how the computations occur.
